legacy_edges.evidence: Both concern LLM-based hypothesis generation in social science; B's finding that LLMs produce high-quality hypotheses supports the premise underlying A's hypothesis-generation method.
Both report that integrating literature-based and data-driven hypothesis generation yields best generalizability/OOD performance with transferable hypotheses — strongly consistent findings.
A evaluates utility of LLM-generated hypotheses for human decisions; both part of HypoGeniC-type research line on hypothesis generation.
B finds augmenting data-driven generation with retrieved literature performs best, supporting A's claim that literature and data hypotheses are complementary.
Both establish gaps between AI agents and human experts on ML research/engineering tasks via benchmarks; RE-Bench's human comparison aligns with PaperBench's human-vs-AI gap finding.
Both compare AI agents to human experts on open-ended ML research tasks; RE-Bench enables exactly the human-vs-agent comparison the other reports.
Both find AI agents are unreliable/lag humans on longer research tasks but occasionally exceed; consistent capability-reliability/time-horizon narrative.
Both inject perturbations/errors into peer review components to diagnose LLM reviewer weaknesses; A is a more structured framework of the general idea B describes.
A perturbation framework diagnoses LLM robustness incl. meta-reviewer role; B finds LLMs fall short at meta-reviewing — A's approach could surface and B's finding agrees on LLM weakness.
Both examine LLM robustness to perturbation/manipulation in peer review; B's finding is an instance of the vulnerability A's framework diagnoses.
Both examine robustness/vulnerability of LLM review systems to perturbation; B quantifies systemic impact while A provides diagnostic framework.
Both concern probing LLM reviewer flaws; B's specific flaw findings are consistent with A's robustness diagnosis aim, though A is a framework not a finding.
B's error-injection method is a means to discover the kind of LLM reviewing blind spots A documents.
Both report LLM shortcomings in meta-reviewing tasks; B's finding that LLMs cannot match human meta-reviewers aligns with A's identified meta-review biases.
Both find LLM reviewers susceptible to manipulation via rebuttal/self-disclosure; B's implicit manipulation finding aligns with A's vulnerability to disclosed weaknesses.
Both document inherent LLM reviewing flaws/biases; B's hallucination and prestige bias findings reinforce A's vulnerability findings.
Both build automated assessment frameworks involving novelty assessment and retrieval; B's DeepReview could incorporate A's evaluation approach.
Both build automated structured peer-review systems emulating expert reviewers; convergent approaches to the same task.
ReviewRL is an RL framework for review generation; DeepReview-13K is a structured review dataset that such a framework could train on, plausibly used as training data.
Both concern LLM-based peer review systems and their evaluation; convergent domain and goals.
ReviewRL is a review-generation framework; DeepReview-Bench evaluates such systems, suggesting ReviewRL could be evaluated on it.
Both develop human-expert-graded benchmarks for LLM-based judges of research quality; corroborating methodologies.
The rubric-free objective evaluation framework appears to address PaperBench's reliance on extensive human rubrics, offering an alternative evaluation approach for the same replication problem.
Both are benchmarks for evaluating ML agents on competition-style ML tasks with performance metrics.
B evaluates AI research agents on ML tasks, complementing A's framework for developing/evaluating such agents.
Both evaluate AI research agents on ML research tasks and report limited agent capabilities; complementary findings.
Both report empirical findings that frontier LLM agents have severe limitations on open-ended AI research tasks, struggling to produce genuine innovation.

A argues LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with effectiveness, undermining LLM-as-judge; B uses multi-dimensional reward models (including novelty and effectiveness) to train an idea agent. There is a tension since A questions the reliability of the very signals B relies on, but they are not directly incompatible claims.
Both identify unreliability of LLM self/judge-evaluation of idea quality; consistent findings.
A claims LLM ideas judged more novel (relying on novelty judgments as meaningful); B argues LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with effectiveness, undermining the reliability of such judgments.

A proposes ground-truth execution to test whether novelty judgments translate to outcomes; B finds LLM novelty judgments poorly correlate with empirical effectiveness. B's finding aligns with the concern A addresses.
Both train models via RL on deep research tasks to better utilize/select research tools; closely aligned in goal and method.
Both are benchmarks for autonomous AI research agents on closed-loop research derived from top venue papers; complementary parallel efforts.
Scientist-Bench is a benchmark for autonomous research agents; B reports agent capability gaps measured on such tasks. Complementary.
Both are benchmarks for autonomous AI research agents; Med-AI Bench extends the benchmark space to medical domain, parallel/complementary to Scientist-Bench.

Both involve mentor-student style guidance for autonomous research code generation from baseline papers/codebases; the refinement architecture could implement Jr. AI Scientist's mentor-guided approach, but link is loose.
Both frame autonomous research as mentor-guided; the refinement architecture mirrors mentor-student collaboration, plausibly an instantiation of the Jr. AI Scientist setting, but tenuous.
Both are hierarchical manuscript composition approaches; B applies a hierarchical composition paradigm in the clinical/medical writing domain, a domain-specific variant of the general approach in A.
Both evaluate AI agents on end-to-end research experiments with subtask-level grading; complementary benchmark and findings.
Both report that leading LLM agents largely fail on end-to-end research tasks, succeeding on code sub-tasks but failing at design and long-horizon planning.

A reports near-zero (0.5%) success of agents on complete executable research experiments; B claims LLM-agent pipelines can complete the full research cycle with executable outcomes. These present conflicting capability assessments.
Both report that LLM agents perform poorly / lack genuine research capability on AI research experiment tasks.

A claims AI feedback can be superior to human reviews; B is a benchmark for evaluating review/feedback generation. Loosely related as B could evaluate the kind of system in A, but distinct contributions.
Both are deep research agent benchmarks; ResearcherBench targets frontier unsolved questions extending the deep research evaluation space beyond DeepResearch Bench.
RLER training method and DeepResearch Bench both about deep research agents; benchmark could evaluate the method.
Both are criteria/rubric-driven evaluation frameworks for research report quality, addressing the same evaluation task with similar dimensional scoring approaches.

Both are automated evaluation methods for open-ended/long-form research report generation aligned with human judgment; they propose alternative approaches to a shared problem, but not directly extending each other.
Both are human-validated automated evaluation methods for open-ended research report generation; complementary approaches to the same problem.
Both relate to benchmarking/operationalizing academic novelty assessment; complementary.
Both concern LLM novelty evaluation; A's benchmarking finding aligns with B's operationalization of novelty assessment.
Both concern LLM novelty evaluation methodology; A's prompting analysis aligns with B's facet operationalization.
Expert-annotated novelty dataset supports evaluation of A's automated novelty report method.
Both are about evaluating novelty; B's expert-annotated dataset could support A's checklist evaluation method, but they are distinct contributions.
A's analysis and fine-tuning strategies for novelty evaluation could build on B's expert-annotated novelty dataset.
Both target improving LLM-based novelty evaluation accuracy via methods grounded in evidence/examples; complementary approaches.
A finds LLMs have limited novelty understanding/gaps with humans; B shows expert in-context examples improve LLM novelty evaluation, consistent with A's finding that LLMs need help.
A identifies prompting strategies improving novelty evaluation; B shows expert in-context examples improve novelty evaluation accuracy — consistent empirical findings.
STELLA's Tool Ocean of bioinformatics tools relates to Biomni-E1's unified environment of 150 tools/databases across 25 domains; STELLA could leverage/extend such an environment.
B reports state-of-the-art accuracy on LAB-Bench DBQA/LitQA, which is exactly the benchmark A introduces; B is an evaluation result on A's benchmark.
Both are reproducibility benchmarks; REPRO-Bench focuses on social science reproduction, related to CORE-Bench's broader reproducibility benchmark.
Both about computational reproducibility evaluation; the fast harness supports running benchmarks like REPRO-Bench efficiently.
A reports poor agent performance on social science reproducibility; B is a social-science reproduction benchmark — same domain, A's results plausibly use such a benchmark.

A claims agents perform below random on social science reproducibility (21.4%); B reports frontier coding agents achieve very high reproducibility (93.4%) on social science findings. These appear to conflict.
B reports results of CORE-Agent on a reproducibility task; directly uses/relates to the CORE benchmark line of work assessing reproducibility.
Both are RL frameworks for scientific review generation with reward models; closely related methods.
B's composite reward combining rule-based and judge-model rewards extends the reward-model approach used in CycleReviewer for review-generation RL.

Both address standardized tool orchestration for scientific AI; an interaction protocol and object-graph mapping could complement, but as stated they're parallel approaches to the same problem, not clearly extending each other.
Both are tooling/metrics for fair, rigorous agent evaluation; complementary methodological contributions.

A claims complete discovery cycles pose novel challenges beyond existing benchmarks; B introduces a replication benchmark for scientific tasks. ReplicationBench could embody or support A's argument about benchmarking discovery, but link is moderate.
Both describe autonomous AI scientist systems generating full papers; A benchmarks such systems while B is one such system. Related theme but distinct artifacts.
Both are environments/benchmarks for evaluating LLM AI-research agents on open-ended tasks; complementary but independent contributions.
Both are benchmarks of open-ended AI research tasks for evaluating research agents; parallel complementary contributions.
A finds LLMs fail to innovate beyond tuning; B's benchmark explicitly rewards innovation over replication, addressing the gap A identifies. Loosely aligned but distinct contributions.
Both named 'ResearchGym' but describe different systems (one a general environment, one a containerized benchmark of five tasks); appear to be conflicting or distinct uses of the same name.
MLGym-Bench provides tasks to evaluate LLM agents on research workflows, consistent with the agent-failure findings; complementary benchmark/evaluation.

Both concern coordinating large numbers of parallel scientific agents for long-horizon autonomous research; alternative coordination strategies (structured world model vs. decentralized self-organization).
Both describe multi-agent architectures for scaling parallel scientific agents; A's structured world model and B's asynchronous framework address the same coordination/scaling problem.

Both describe autonomous AI scientist systems producing discoveries; B's scaling result on discovery cycles is consistent with and supports the feasibility claim of A, though they are different systems.
Both report autonomous AI scientists achieving validated quality scientific output, broadly consistent evidence for AI-driven discovery feasibility.
Both concern evaluating automated peer-review quality against human reviews, but A is an analysis and B is a metric; loosely related.
Both are automated peer-review models claiming strong performance versus humans/baselines; same research thrust.
A is an automated review system; B is an evaluation benchmark suite for automated peer review tasks; complementary.
Both are benchmark/execution environments evaluating AI agents on research tasks; complementary parallel efforts.
Both concern benchmarks/evaluation of AI research agents on open-ended ML research with end-to-end assessment.
Both concern multi-agent approaches improving scientific idea generation; A's findings support B's self-evolution mechanism premise.
Both report multi-agent systems improving scientific idea generation quality over baselines; consistent findings, though different systems.
A identifies result fabrication/validation failure as a barrier; B's self-debugging verification loop directly addresses validity of synthesized tasks, supporting the motivation.
A introduces MLGym-Bench; B reports improvements on the MLGym benchmark, so B uses A's benchmark.
A introduces the AUP metric; B reports results measured on the AUP metric, so B uses/depends on A's metric.

A's asynchronous multi-GPU infrastructure makes evolutionary ML search tractable; B demonstrates evolutionary code optimization delivering gains across compute stacks — A provides enabling infrastructure consistent with B's approach.
A establishes score prediction as the benchmark; B explicitly withholds accept-reject decisions and rejects paper-scoring framing — genuine tension.
A reports agents fabricate/fail to validate results; B argues outcome evaluation misses reasoning failures and reasoning must be targeted. Both highlight limits of outcome reliability.
B is a large corpus of AI-generated ideas; A's predictor could use such a corpus, but link is speculative.
B is a corpus of AI-generated ideas; A's ranking method could be applied to such a corpus, but speculative.

Both are automated evaluation frameworks for AI-generated research validated to align with human experts; MLR-Judge's approach of LLM reviewers matching human agreement supports the feasibility of the multi-signal protocol's human-validated judgement.

Both document systematic failure modes of LLM research/ideation agents. Different specific failures (diversity/self-eval vs. evidence-decision decoupling) but consistent in showing systematic agent limitations.
MLEvolve is a more elaborate self-evolving multi-agent ML discovery framework that generalizes/extends the tree-search code optimization paradigm pioneered by AIDE.
A organizes solution search as a tree of executable scripts; MCGS directly extends tree search with cross-branch graph edges and progressive schedule, addressing exactly the isolation in such trees.
A reports tree-search code optimization achieving SOTA; MCGS is an improved tree/graph search method — both evidence the value of search-based code optimization, plausibly the same line of work.
A uses agentic tree search for open-ended code/hypothesis exploration; MCGS is a concrete improvement to tree-based search that A's approach could employ.
B refines the solution-tree search by decoupling planning from code generation and adding editing-mode selection, improving the iteration described in A.
AlphaEvolve uses LLM-driven code edits guided by evaluation; B refines code-editing strategy (rewrite/stepwise/diff) for code optimization agents — same domain, B refines the edit mechanism.
Both concern long-horizon code optimization agents; A's tree-search execution and B's editing-mode selection are complementary components of such agents.
B claims to outperform AlphaEvolve on math algorithm optimization tasks; A is a related AlphaEvolve-style math result, but no direct comparison stated between these two specifically. Weak relation.
Both assess AI/automated peer review capability relative to human reviewers, broadly agreeing AI can contribute to peer review.
PaperQA2 is explicitly the successor agent extending PaperQA's RAG tool-based design.
PaperQA2 is evaluated on full-literature retrieval tasks like LitQA; the benchmark supports evaluation of such agents. Same lineage (LitQA used to evaluate PaperQA).
Both describe agent-based RAG systems for scientific literature that match or exceed expert/strong-LLM performance; B (PaperQA2) is likely the same or closely related system as A.
A describes a RAG agent matching expert humans in accuracy/time at lower cost; B (PaperQA2) is the agent achieving expert-level literature performance. Strongly aligned, likely same work.
B provides the human-AI comparison methodology with unrestricted human baselines used to establish A's claim of matching experts in accuracy and time.
B's finding that researchers perceive LLM feedback as helpful supports the value of systems like MARG that generate review feedback.

B's synthetic difficulty benchmark evaluates hypothesis discovery methods like HypoGeniC; same research line (HypoBench-related).
